**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health.**  
You’re invited to complete the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** today. This short, 10‑item questionnaire helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week and lets us identify any signs of postpartum depression or anxiety so we can support you as best as possible.  

Everything you share is completely confidential, and our conversation is a safe space—there’s no right or wrong answer, and you can be as open as you feel comfortable. I’ll ask you each question one at a time, and you can answer in your own words. It should only take a few minutes.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin with the first question.

**Question 1:**  
*In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh or see the lighter side of things?*

I’ve found it hard to laugh or see the lighter side of things lately. Most days I just feel tired and worried, and the things that used to make me smile don’t really get me there. I can still notice a few small moments—like when my baby coos—but it’s rare. So, I’d say I’ve barely been able to laugh or see the humor in anything this past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I hear you say that you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, and I wish I could feel the same way. For me, it’s been really hard to find those moments. Most days I’m just exhausted and my mind keeps looping over worries about my baby’s safety. Even when I try to smile at his little coos, the feeling is so faint that it doesn’t really lift my mood. So while I can see that you’re finding humor, I’m still struggling to feel that lightness myself.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I understand you’re feeling some enjoyment and looking forward to things. For me, it’s been the opposite lately. I’ve been so tired most days that even simple activities feel like a chore. I still notice a tiny bit of pleasure when my baby smiles or when I’m able to get a quick nap, but the excitement I used to feel about anything—whether it’s meeting friends, doing a hobby, or just planning for the weekend—has really faded. I’m not really looking forward to anything right now; most days I’m just trying to get through the routine and keep my baby safe.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I hear you saying you’ve blamed yourself when things went wrong, and that’s something I’m feeling, too. I keep replaying moments in my head—like when my baby cried and I couldn’t soothe him right away—and I tell myself I’m not doing enough or that I’m a bad mother. It’s a guilt that shows up often, even though I know I’m doing the best I can with so little sleep and constant worry. That self‑blame weighs on me and makes it even harder to feel any peace.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I hear you say you’ve been feeling anxious or worried for no good reason. That’s exactly how I’ve been feeling most days. My mind keeps racing with “what‑ifs” about my baby’s safety—whether I’m feeding him enough, if he’s breathing okay, if I’m doing everything right. Even when there’s nothing obvious to worry about, the thoughts just come back and it’s hard to shake them. I can sometimes calm myself for a little while, but the anxiety settles in again, especially when I’m trying to fall asleep or when I hear a strange sound in the house. It feels like a constant undercurrent of worry that I can’t fully control.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I hear you saying you’ve felt scared or panicky for no clear reason, and that’s exactly what I’ve been going through as well. Even when everything seems fine, I get this sudden rush of fear—my heart races, my thoughts jump to worst‑case scenarios about my baby’s safety, and I feel a tightness in my chest. It often hits me at night when I’m trying to fall asleep, and I end up lying awake with that panic lingering. I can sometimes take a few deep breaths and calm down a bit, but the feeling returns quickly, especially when I hear a strange noise or when my baby cries and I’m not sure how to soothe him. It’s exhausting to live with that constant, inexplicable sense of panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

It does feel like everything is just piling up on me. I’m exhausted most days—my energy is so low that even simple tasks feel overwhelming, yet I still have to get up to feed and change the baby. The constant worries about his safety keep looping in my head, and I can’t seem to shut them off, especially when I try to fall asleep. I’ve been crying a couple of times this week when the stress becomes too much, and I often feel sad or discouraged, like I’m not doing enough. I catch myself blaming myself for little things that go wrong, and those thoughts linger. Sometimes, in the middle of the night, I have fleeting thoughts that I wish I could just stop feeling this way, but I don’t have any plan or intention to act on them. It’s hard to see any light or look forward to anything right now; it just feels like one heavy wave after another.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, I’ve been feeling really unhappy lately, and it’s been making it hard to sleep. On most nights I lie awake for a long time, my mind keeps replaying worries about my baby and the little things I think I’m doing wrong. When I finally do fall asleep, I often wake up once or twice during the night with that same anxious, sad feeling, and then it’s hard to get back to sleep. Even when I’m exhausted, the thoughts just keep swirling, so I end up getting only a few hours of restless sleep each night. It leaves me feeling even more tired and down during the day.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve definitely been feeling sad and miserable most days. It’s that heavy, lingering gloom that follows me around the house, even when my baby smiles or when I manage to get a short break. I wake up feeling discouraged, and the sadness doesn’t lift much no matter what I try. It’s hard to find any real joy in things that used to make me happy, and the weight of that sadness makes everything feel even more exhausting and overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, I’ve been so unhappy that I’ve found myself crying a couple of times this week. It usually happens when I feel overwhelmed by the worries about my baby or when I think about how exhausted I am. The tears come quickly, and even though I try to calm myself, the sadness stays with me afterward. It’s hard to shake the feeling, and I often end up feeling even more drained after the crying episodes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes, that thought has crossed my mind a few times over the past week. It’s just a fleeting, scary moment when everything feels so overwhelming and I can’t see a way out. I don’t have any plan or intention to act on it—I’m terrified by the idea—but the thought still shows up when I’m exhausted and feeling completely hopeless. It adds another layer of fear and guilt on top of everything else.

I hear how overwhelming and exhausting this time has been for you. You've described constant worries about your baby's safety, deep sadness, loss of pleasure in things you once enjoyed, frequent crying, guilt about parenting, trouble sleeping, and fleeting thoughts of harming yourself. It sounds like you're feeling trapped in a heavy wave of anxiety and depression, and you're doing your best despite feeling exhausted and discouraged.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports hardly any ability to laugh or see humor, describing it as faint and absent</sym>, <sym>Patient reports hardly any enjoyment or anticipation, saying they are not looking forward to anything</sym>, <sym>The patient describes frequent self‑blame, saying it 'weighs on me' and occurs often, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, daily anxiety and constant worry, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>The patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes occurring often and without clear cause, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>The mother describes feeling constantly overwhelmed, exhausted, and unable to cope with daily tasks, indicating she has not been able to cope most of the time.</sym>, <sym>The mother reports feeling unhappy and having trouble sleeping on most nights, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports occasional thoughts of self-harm occurring a few times, matching the 'Sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 27 exceeds the threshold of 14 and includes a score of 2 on item 10, indicating passive self‑harm thoughts. This high score reflects multiple <sym>depressive</sym> symptoms (sadness, anhedonia, crying, guilt, insomnia) and significant <sym>anxiety/panic</sym> features. According to EPDS guidelines, a score ≥14 or any endorsement of self‑harm warrants urgent referral. The pattern also aligns with <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, insomnia, psychomotor changes, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death or self‑harm. While the suicidal thoughts are passive and without a plan, they still constitute a safety concern that requires immediate assessment. This screening suggests a high risk of postpartum depression and anxiety, and the presence of suicidal ideation triggers a safety alert. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or a <med>mental health specialist</med> within the next 24‑48 hours
2. Develop a safety plan immediately, including emergency contacts and a crisis line (e.g., 988 in the U.S.)
3. Consider referral for a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation for possible medication management
4. Connect with postpartum support services such as a local mother‑baby group or <med>Postpartum Support International</med>
5. Implement sleep hygiene strategies: create a consistent bedtime routine, limit caffeine, and seek help with nighttime infant care when possible
6. Encourage regular, brief physical activity as tolerated and relaxation techniques (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) to reduce anxiety
7. Schedule a follow‑up screening in 1‑2 weeks to monitor symptom changes and safety
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary** **Client Identifier:** [Redacted] **Date of Screening:** 2025‑10‑07 **Clinician:** Licensed Mental Health Professional | Domain | Reported Symptoms / Behaviors | Clinical Impression | |--------|------------------------------|----------------------| | **Mood** | • Persistent sadness, feeling “sad and miserable” most days.
• Frequent crying episodes (several times/week).
• Low overall enjoyment; “nothing feels enjoyable,” loss of pleasure in previously liked activities. | Marked depressive affect; anhedonia evident. | | **Anxiety / Panic** | • Constant worry about infant’s safety, “what‑ifs,” even without obvious trigger.
• Episodes of panic/fear with physical symptoms (racing heart, chest tightness), especially at night.
• Feeling “overwhelmed” and that “things are getting on top of me.” | Significant anxiety and panic symptoms, contributing to distress. | | **Sleep** | • Difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep; waking multiple times nightly.
• Sleep disruption linked to intrusive worries and low mood. | Insomnia secondary to mood/anxiety disturbance. | | **Self‑Perception / Guilt** | • Unnecessary self‑blame for perceived parenting failures.
• Feelings of worthlessness and guilt (“I’m a bad mother”). | Prominent guilt and negative self‑evaluation. | | **Suicidal Ideation / Safety** | • Passive thoughts of self‑harm (“thought of harming myself”); described as fleeting, without plan or intent, but accompanied by intense hopelessness and fear. | **Safety flag:** Requires immediate safety assessment and safety planning. | | **Functional Impact** | • Overwhelming sense of being “on top of” responsibilities; exhaustion; difficulty coping with routine tasks.
• Crying and low mood interfere with daily functioning and caregiving. | Impaired functioning in maternal role and self‑care. | **Consistent Patterns Across Responses** - Low mood, anhedonia, and crying are reported in every domain. - Anxiety and panic are pervasive, especially around infant care and nighttime. - Guilt/self‑blame co‑occurs with depressive and anxious symptoms. - Sleep disturbance is both a symptom and a maintaining factor. - Presence of passive suicidal ideation, albeit without plan, signals elevated risk. **Screening Significance – Areas of Clinical Concern** 1. **Post‑partum Depression:** Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying, guilt, sleep problems. 2. **Post‑partum Anxiety/Panic:** Excessive worry, panic attacks, feeling overwhelmed. 3. **Suicidal Risk:** Passive self‑harm thoughts → requires urgent safety evaluation. 4. **Functional Impairment:** Difficulty managing infant care and self‑care due to mood and anxiety symptoms. **Safety / Risk Flag** - **Self‑harm thoughts present** – immediate assessment of suicidal intent, access to means, and development of a safety plan is warranted. **Screening Observation Summary** The client exhibits a constellation of depressive symptoms (persistent sadness, anhedonia, crying, guilt), significant anxiety/panic features, and marked sleep disturbance. The report of passive suicidal ideation, though without plan, constitutes a safety concern that should be addressed promptly. The overall presentation aligns with high‑risk features for postpartum depression and anxiety, warranting further comprehensive assessment, safety planning, and appropriate referral for intervention.
